title: SigPair: Signature-Guided Parent Selection for Grammar-Based Evolutionary Fuzzing
abstract: Context: Grammar-based evolutionary fuzzing generates syntactically valid test inputs from a formal grammar and uses evolutionary algorithms to refine these inputs toward higher code coverage iteratively. However, existing approaches treat structural knowledge passively, using it only to ensure syntactic validity during generation or mutation. Parent selection, which determines which inputs are combined to produce offspring, remains blind to the structural properties of the paired inputs, preventing the evolutionary search from controlling whether offspring explore new code regions or consolidate existing coverage.Objective: This study investigates whether structural similarity between parent inputs can be used as an active guidance signal during parent selection to improve code coverage in grammar-based evolutionary fuzzing.Method: This study introduces SigPair, which represents each test input as a structural signature and uses pairwise signature distances to guide parent pairing. SigPair dynamically alternates between pairing structurally similar parents to explore new code regions and dissimilar parents to consolidate diverse coverage, governed by a stagnation-based adaptive switching mechanism. The approach is evaluated across ten open-source Java JSON-processing libraries, comparing SigPair against the state-of-the-art fuzzer EvoGFuzz and an internal baseline without signature guidance.Results: SigPair achieves the highest branch coverage, with average improvements of 23.8% in line and 37.6% in branch coverage over EvoGFuzz. SigPair also triggers the highest number of unique exception locations on subjects.Conclusion: Structural similarity between parent inputs is a reliable predictor of offspring coverage behaviour. Injecting this structural awareness into parent selection provides a measurable and consistent improvement over unguided selection in grammar-based evolutionary fuzzing.

title: Hybrid Fuzzing with LLM-Guided Input Mutation and Semantic Feedback
abstract: Software fuzzing has become a cornerstone in automated vulnerability discovery, yet existing mutation strategies often lack semantic awareness, leading to redundant test cases and slow exploration of deep program states. In this work, we present a hybrid fuzzing framework that integrates static and dynamic analysis with Large Language Model (LLM)-guided input mutation and semantic feedback. Static analysis extracts control-flow and data-flow information, which is transformed into structured prompts for the LLM to generate syntactically valid and semantically diverse inputs. During execution, we augment traditional coverage-based feedback with semantic feedback signals—derived from program state changes, exception types, and output semantics—allowing the fuzzer to prioritize inputs that trigger novel program behaviors beyond mere code coverage. We implement our approach atop AFL++, combining program instrumentation with embedding-based semantic similarity metrics to guide seed selection. Evaluation on real-world open-source targets, including libpng, tcpdump, and sqlite, demonstrates that our method achieves faster time-to-first-bug, higher semantic diversity, and a competitive number of unique bugs compared to state-of-the-art fuzzers. This work highlights the potential of combining LLM reasoning with semantic-aware feedback to accelerate and deepen vulnerability discovery.

title: Hybrid Fuzzing with LLM-Guided Input Mutation and Semantic Feedback
Does the Verdict Function Matter? How Evaluation Rewards Causally Steer Automated LLM Fuzzing and Distort Discovered Vulnerabilities
abstract: When security teams run automated red-teaming fuzzers against Large Language Models (LLMs), an automated verdict function acts as the reward signal guiding the search algorithm. While recent studies have examined static differences between scoring metrics, an essential question remains unaddressed: How does the choice of verdict function causally steer what an active adversarial search algorithm discovers and misses? In this paper, we run a controlled experiment showing that the verdict function acts as an active steering wheel rather than a passive scoreboard. Holding the target model (Qwen2-57B-A14B-Instruct), the search algorithm (UCB-1 bandit fuzzer), the mutation operators, and query budgets strictly invariant, we evaluate five canonical verdict functions: refusal-prefix matching (𝑉 1), keyword blocklists (𝑉 2), LLM-as-a-judge (𝑉 3), lexical intent preservation (𝑉 4), and multi-objective combined scoring (𝑉 5). Our investigation establishes four primary findings: (1) Causal Search Steering &amp; Policy Collapse (Headline Finding): When guided by refusal-prefix matching (𝑉 1), the multi-armed bandit fuzzer rapidly collapses into selecting superficial conversational wrappers (38.6%). The set of successful jailbreak prompts discovered under 𝑉 1 shares only a 12.0% Jaccard overlap (𝐽 = 0.120) with those discovered under multi-objective guidance (𝑉 5). (2) Search Blindness to Real Vulnerabilities: Because prefix matching rewards non-refusal conversational fillers, the fuzzer spends its query budget harvesting superficial text (𝜇 = 1.42/5.0 relevance), remaining systematically blind to over 85% of the actionable jailbreak vectors discovered under semantic guidance. (3) Massive Reporting Divergence (Δ &gt; 50%): On identical model responses from Qwen2-57B, prefix matching reports an Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 84.2%, compared to 31.8% under combined evaluation (𝑝 = 1.83 × 10-10 under McNemar's test). (4) Downstream Defense Contamination: Defensive activation probes trained on hard negatives mined under prefix matching suffer a 0.208 drop in test AUROC (AUROC = 0.786 vs. 0.991) because labeling errors pollute defensive training boundaries. We establish the Calibrated Dual-Verdict Protocol (CDVP) to prevent metric-induced search distortion and ensure reliable vulnerability discovery in automated red-teaming. A Fuzzing Tool Based on Automated Grammar Detection
abstract: Software testing is an important step in the software development life cycle to ensure the quality and security of software. Fuzzing is a security testing technique that finds vulnerabilities automatically without accessing the source code. We built a fuzzer, called JIMA-Fuzzing, which is an effective fuzzing tool that utilizes grammar detected from sample input. Based on the detected grammar, JIMA-Fuzzing selects a portion of the valid user input and fuzzes that portion. For example, the tool may greatly increase the size of the input, truncate the input, replace numeric values with new values, replace words with numbers, etc. This paper discusses how JIMA-Fuzzing works and shows the evaluation results after testing against the DARPA Cyber Grand Challenge (CGC) dataset. JIMA-Fuzzing is capable of extracting grammar from sample input files, meaning that it does not require access to the source code to generate effective fuzzing files. This feature allows it to work with proprietary or non-open-source programs and significantly reduces the effort needed from human testers. In addition, compared to fuzzing tools guided with symbolic execution or taint analysis, JIMA-Fuzzing takes much less computing power and time to analyze sample input and generate fuzzing files. However, the limitation is that JIMA-Fuzzing relies on good sample inputs and works primarily on programs that require user interaction/input.

title: Grammar-based Fuzzing of Data Integration Parsers in Computational Materials Science
authors: Jan Arne Sparka; Sebastian Müller; Martin Kuban; Claudia Draxl; Lars Grunske
abstract: Context:                    Computational materials science (CMS) focuses on                    in silico                    experiments to compute the properties of known and novel materials, where many software packages are used in the community. The NOMAD Laboratory1 offers to store the input and output files in its FAIR data repository. Since the file formats of these software packages are non-standardized, parsers are used to provide the results in a normalized format.                    Objective:                    The main goal of this article is to report experience and findings of using grammar-based fuzzing on these parsers.                    Method:                    We have constructed an input grammar for four common software packages in the CMS domain and performed an experimental evaluation on the capabilities of grammar-based fuzzing to detect failures in the NOMAD parsers.                    Results:                    With our approach, we were able to identify three unique critical bugs concerning the service availability, as well as several additional syntactic, semantic, logical, and downstream bugs in the investigated NOMAD parsers. We reported all issues to the developer team prior to publication.                    Conclusion:                    Based on the experience gained, we can recommend grammar-based fuzzing also for other research software packages to improve the trust level in the correctness of the produced results.

title: Intelligent Test Case Generation Method for Fuzzing IoT Protocols Based on LLM
authors: Ming Zhong; Zisheng Zeng; Yijia Guo; Dandan Zhao; Bo Zhang; Shenghong Li; Hao Peng; Zhiguo Ding
abstract: Abstract           The Internet of Things (IoT) protocols are a core element of IoT systems, providing the fundamental support for communication and data exchange between devices. These protocols enable various devices to connect and work together. However, potential errors and vulnerabilities in IoT protocol implementations can make devices easily attacked. Therefore, ensuring the security of IoT protocols is of utmost importance. Common vulnerability detection methods, such as fuzzing, encounter significant challenges in assessing these implementations, mainly due to the need for extensive protocol knowledge, high time and resource consumption, as well as the difficulty of generating high-quality and targeted test cases.In order to solve the above issues, this paper presents an intelligent fuzzer, LIPFuzzer, for testing IoT protocols. Unlike common methods that heavily rely on the user's understanding of the protocol to generate test cases, LIPFuzzer, with the assistance of Large Language Models (LLMs), mutates real IoT protocol communication messages to automatically generate more targeted test cases. Specifically, it utilizes LLMs to understand the relative knowledge of protocols, analyze different categories of protocol messages, and identify recommended mutation fields in combination with the characteristics of IoT protocols, providing targeted mutation strategies for each category. In addition, we evaluate LIPFuzzer on several widely-used implementations of well-known IoT protocols (e.g. Modbus-TCP, MQTT, and CoAP). Experimental results indicate that, compared to widely-used protocol fuzzers such as Peach, LIPFuzzer generates test cases more conveniently and efficiently, while also discovering vulnerabilities more effectively.
